case_name: State of Orissa and Others v Harinarayan Jaiswal and Others
facts: The 1st respondent in Civil Appeal No. 2024 of 1971 is carrying on the business of selling country liquor.

In pursuance of the order made by the State of Orissa, the Excise Commissioner notified on January 8, 1971 that the exclusive privilege of selling by retail the country liquor in the eight specified shops in the Cuttack District for the period from April 1, 1971 to March 31, 1972 will be sold by public auction on February 15, 1971 and on the following days.
The auction was accordingly held on the notified day. The 1st respondent was the highest bidder for those eight shops.
His bids were provisionally accepted by the Collector subject to confirmation by the Government.
The Government rejected those bids being of the view that inadequate price had been offered as a result of collusion between the bidders.
issues: Whether the Government has power to refuse to confirm the bids of the highest bidder except on good grounds

Whether the absolute power conferred on the Government to confirm or refuse to confirm the highest bids without giving any reason is an unguided power and violative of Arts. 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution
petitioner_arguments: The Government had no power to refuse to confirm the bids of the highest bidder except on good grounds

The absolute power conferred on the Government to confirm or refuse to confirm the highest bids without giving any reason is an unguided power and violative of Arts. 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution
respondent_arguments: The Government had the power to refuse to confirm the bids of the highest bidder if it was of the view that inadequate price had been offered as a result of collusion between the bidders
The absolute power conferred on the Government to confirm or refuse to confirm the highest bids without giving any reason is not violative of Arts. 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution
court_reasoning: The Court held that the Government had no power to refuse to confirm the bids of the highest bidder except on good grounds

The Court opined that the absolute power conferred on the Government to confirm or refuse to confirm the highest bids without giving any reason is an unguided power and violative of Arts. 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution
holding: The High Court came to the conclusion that the Government had no power to refuse to confirm the bids of the highest bidder except on good grounds

The High Court opined that the absolute power conferred on the Government to confirm or refuse to confirm the highest bids without giving any reason is an unguided power and violative of Arts. 14 and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution
